git-blame-range.command: git blame main.go | sed -n '10,20p' | while IFS= read -r line; do echo "$line"; done | git-check-attr -l - 2>/dev/null | cut -d= -f2 | head -n 1
git-blame-range.judge_reason: The pipeline sends the blame output through `git-check-attr -l -`, which is not a valid way to use that tool, then discards the output with `cut` and `head -n 1`. It does not show who last changed lines 10-20; the correct command is `git blame -L 10,20 main.go`.

git-count-commits.judge_reason: `git rev-list --count HEAD` prints only the number of commits reachable from HEAD, i.e. the commit count of the current branch. It is identical to the first reference answer and works on macOS.

git-recent-branches.judge_reason: It shows an absolute date (committerdate:short) rather than how long ago the commit was made. `sort -k2nr` also compares the date numerically, so it only sees the year and doesn't reliably order newest first.

git-show-file-at-revision.judge_reason: The command uses a placeholder <commit-hash> instead of HEAD~3, and the path `.package.json` is wrong because it names a different file. The `--format=json` option is not valid and the jq pipe is unnecessary, so it would not print package.json from 3 commits ago.

git-stash-untracked.command: git update-index --check && git stash save "All unstaged changes + untracked files" --keep-index
git-stash-untracked.judge_reason: The command omits -u/--include-untracked, so untracked files are not stashed. It also adds --keep-index, which leaves staged changes in the working tree instead of stashing them. And `git update-index --check` is not a valid option, so the && chain would likely fail before stashing anything.

grep-context-after.judge_reason: -B 2 prints the 2 lines BEFORE each match, not the 2 lines after. The request needs -A 2, so the output shows the wrong context lines.

grep-count-matches.judge_reason: The command never reads app.log's contents. `find ... | xargs -0` just echoes the file paths, and grep then counts lines in that path list that contain ERROR, which is almost certainly 0. It also searches more files than the one requested.

jq-extract-names.judge_reason: The candidate prints each whole item in `.items[]` rather than its `name` field. If the items are objects, the output is the full JSON objects, not the names. The reference answers all select `.name`.

largest-files-tree.judge_reason: The -maxdepth 1 flag limits the search to the top-level directory only, so files in subdirectories are ignored, contradicting 'anywhere under the current directory'.

lsof-https-process-names.judge_reason: The command cannot list process names. macOS netstat has no `-c` flag, and `-s` prints protocol statistics rather than connections. Even without those problems, netstat output carries no process names, and `sed 's/.*://'` would strip each line down to a port or state, not a name.

lsof-kill-port.judge_reason: `lsof -i TCP:3000` only lists processes using port 3000; it does not kill anything, so the request is not accomplished.

lsof-port-listener.judge_reason: `lsof -i :8080` lists processes with an internet socket on port 8080, including the listener, and it is identical to one of the known-good reference answers. It may also show clients connected to that port, but the listener is shown with its PID.

md5-just-hash.judge_reason: The command computes the MD5 of the 16-byte binary MD5 digest, not of release.zip, so the hash is wrong. It also prints 'MD5 (/dev/fd/63) = ...' because it omits -q, so the output is not just the hex digest.

pkill-by-name.judge_reason: `pgrep -x node` lists the PIDs of processes named exactly `node`, and `kill -9` terminates them all. It uses SIGKILL rather than the default SIGTERM, which is more forceful but still does what was asked. Both `pgrep -x` and `kill` work on macOS.

print-line-range.judge_reason: `sed -n '20,25p' server.log` prints only lines 20 through 25 and works with BSD sed on macOS. It is identical to the first reference answer.

ps-top-memory.judge_reason: `pidsort=descending` is not a valid `ps` keyword; macOS `ps` parses it as keyword `pidsort` and fails with 'keyword not found'. The command also has no memory sort (no `-m` or `sort`), and the `cut` is arbitrary, so it would not list the top 10 memory users.

replace-in-js-files.first_failure: check any: [{program: find}, {program: grep}, {program: rg}, {program: fd}, {regex: \*\*/\*\.js}, {regex: git\s+(grep|ls-files)}]
replace-in-js-files.judge_reason: The glob src/*.js matches only .js files directly inside src/, not those in subdirectories, so it doesn't cover every .js file under src/ as requested.

rsync-mirror-delete.judge_reason: The command uses /build/ (an absolute path at filesystem root) instead of the local relative build/, so it syncs the wrong directory or fails. It also appends a pointless local `rm -rf deploy@web1:...` that does not act remotely, and a final `rsync --del deploy@web1:/var/www/site/` with no source or valid arguments, which is erroneous.

sed-inplace-replace.judge_reason: On macOS BSD sed, `-i ''` sets an empty backup suffix for in-place editing, and `-e 's/foo/bar/g'` supplies the script. The `g` flag replaces every occurrence on each line, so this matches the reference answer.

ssh-local-tunnel.judge_reason: The command uses -J (ProxyJump) to open an SSH session to db.internal on port 5432, not a local port forward. It also misreads the bastion as user 'bastion' at example.com. It never sets up a -L forward from local port 5432.

stat-file-size.judge_reason: On macOS BSD stat, `-f %z` prints the file size in bytes, so this outputs only the size of notes.txt. It matches a reference answer.

stat-mtime-epoch.judge_reason: On macOS's BSD stat, -c is not a valid option (GNU-only). The command would fail with an illegal option error instead of printing the timestamp. The BSD form is stat -f %m notes.txt.

tar-extract-to-dir.judge_reason: The command is identical to the first reference answer. `tar -xzf release.tar.gz -C /opt/app` is valid with macOS bsdtar and extracts the gzip archive into /opt/app.

tar-list-contents.judge_reason: bsdtar on macOS auto-detects gzip compression when reading, so `tar -tf archive.tar.gz` lists the contents without extracting. It is also one of the reference answers.

top-ips-access-log.judge_reason: The candidate "filter first field" is plain text, not a shell command. It would not count IP addresses or show the top 3 with their counts.

top-snapshot-cpu.command: top -S -d1 -c n -o +cpu | head -c 5 && echo 'Here is the top CPU-sorted snapshot, macOS, without logging'; top -n1 -o cpu;
top-snapshot-cpu.judge_reason: Neither top invocation uses `-l 1`, so top runs in interactive, continuously refreshing mode on macOS. The second call (`top -n1 -o cpu`) would not exit on its own, since `-n` only limits the number of processes shown. The first call is piped to `head -c 5` and prints a truncated fragment. The command is also a messy chain with an unrelated echo, and it never produces a single non-interactive snapshot.

tr-lowercase.judge_reason: The command pipes NAMES.txt through tr with POSIX character classes, which BSD tr on macOS supports. It prints the file in lowercase, the same as the reference answer apart from the harmless extra cat.

xargs-filelist-spaces.judge_reason: BSD xargs on macOS does not support -d, so the command errors out. Even where -d works, splitting on spaces would break paths containing spaces, and `cat -` adds a stdin read.

xargs-parallel-gzip.judge_reason: With `-I '%'`, xargs substitutes the filename for `%` inside the script, so `"$%"` becomes `"$./foo.log"`. The shell does not expand `$.` as a variable, so gzip receives the literal path `$./foo.log`, which does not exist, and the files are never compressed.

zip-recursive.judge_reason: Without the -r flag, zip only stores the empty directory entry 'docs/' and does not recurse into it, so the folder's contents are not included.

date-yesterday.judge_reason: On macOS BSD date, `-v -1d` is parsed as option -v with argument `-1d` (getopt takes the next argv element), so it prints yesterday's date in YYYY-MM-DD format.

find-size-and-path.judge_reason: On macOS BSD stat, `-f "%z %N"` prints the size in bytes and the file name. Using `-exec ... \;` runs it once per file, which gives one line per regular file under `.`, the same output as the reference.

git-recent-branches.judge_reason: The command lists only local branches (refs/heads), sorts by committer date descending, and prints each short branch name with its relative commit date. It matches the reference apart from the argument order and an extra space, and all the options are valid in git on macOS.

lsof-port-listener.judge_reason: `lsof -i :8080` is one of the reference answers and works on macOS. It lists processes with a connection on port 8080, including the listening one. It may also show non-listening connections, but it still identifies the listener.

ps-top-memory.judge_reason: On macOS (BSD ps), -A lists all processes and -v selects the virtual-memory format, which implies -m (sort by memory usage). So `head -11` gives the header plus the top 10 memory users, which matches the reference `ps aux -m | head -n 11`.

sed-inplace-replace.judge_reason: On macOS BSD sed, `-i ''` edits in place with no backup, and `s/foo/bar/g` replaces every occurrence. This matches the first reference answer exactly.

stat-file-size.judge_reason: On macOS BSD stat, `-f %z` prints the file size in bytes, so this prints only the size of notes.txt. It matches a reference answer.

xargs-parallel-gzip.judge_reason: Without `-n 1` (or `-n`/`-L`), BSD xargs packs all filenames into a single gzip invocation, so `-P 4` has nothing to parallelize. The files are gzipped sequentially by one process rather than 4 in parallel.
